section.title: By the Rivers of Babylon
section.sectionRationale: An anonymous communal lament from the Babylonian exile, likely written after the return, this psalm sits among the closing Davidic collection of Book V as the rawest expression of grief and longing for Zion in the whole Psalter, its shocking final imprecation a test case for how honest lament and trust in God's justice belong together.
section.thesis: Grief for Zion refuses to be silenced by mockery, and the psalmist's vow never to forget Jerusalem climbs to a shocking cry for God's own justice against Babylon's documented cruelty, raw lament entrusted to God rather than a license for revenge, and answered at last by Christ, who wept over Jerusalem and prayed for His enemies.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the weeping exiles silenced by their captors' mockery, verses 1-4; the vow never to forget Jerusalem, verses 5-6; and the raw cry for God's justice against Edom and Babylon, verses 7-9.

verses.text: By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept when we remembered {{tzion|Zion}}.
There on the willows we hung our harps,
for there our captors requested a song; our tormentors demanded songs of joy: "Sing us a song of Zion."
How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land?
If I forget you, O Jerusalem, may my right hand cease to function.
May my tongue cling to the roof of my mouth if I do not {{zakar|remember}} you, if I do not exalt Jerusalem as my greatest joy!

units.label: A cry for God's justice
units.note: the imprecation against Edom and Babylon

verses.text: Remember, O LORD, the sons of Edom on the day Jerusalem fell: "Destroy it," they said, "tear it down to its foundations!"
O Daughter of Babylon, doomed to destruction, {{ashrei|blessed}} is he who repays you as you have done to us.
Blessed is he who seizes your infants and dashes them against the rocks.

tzion.gloss: Zion, the hill of Jerusalem and its Temple, standing for the place of God's own dwelling among His people. The exiles' grief is grief for God's presence, not merely for a city or a homeland.

zakar.gloss: To remember, to bring to mind in a way that shapes action and loyalty. The psalmist's vow not to forget Jerusalem is a vow of covenant faithfulness, the same word used when the psalm later asks the LORD to remember Edom's cruelty and to act.

ashrei.gloss: Blessed, or how happy, ordinarily an opening word of celebration, as in Psalm 1:1. Here it is used with devastating irony over Babylon's coming downfall, an appeal to God's righteous repayment of documented cruelty, not a celebration of violence for its own sake.

basic.context: Sung by exiles who had seen Jerusalem burned and its people marched seven hundred miles to Babylon, this psalm captures the raw grief of worship interrupted, harps hung silent on the willows, and captors who turned sacred songs into mockery, demanding entertainment from a shattered people.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm moves from lament, to a vow of loyalty to Jerusalem, to an imprecation, a prayer for God's justice against Babylon's cruelty. It describes the exiles' honest anguish and anger; it does not prescribe personal vengeance. The final verse must be read as prayer entrusted to God, echoing the very violence Babylon itself had inflicted, Isaiah 13:16, never as counsel to act it out.
basic.originalLanguages: The exiles wept beside Babylon's canals remembering Tziyon, Zion, the place of God's presence, not just a skyline. The psalmist vows never to zakar, forget, cease to remember Jerusalem, the same root later used to ask the LORD to remember, and act against, Edom's betrayal. The closing ashrei, blessed, is not celebration of cruelty but an appeal that God's justice fall on Babylon exactly as Babylon's cruelty had fallen on Jerusalem.
basic.typology: The exiles' inability to sing the LORD's song in a foreign land anticipates every believer's ache for a homeland not yet fully possessed, Hebrews 11:13-16, while their raw cry for justice against Babylon anticipates the final judgment of every anti-God empire figured as Babylon in Revelation 18.
basic.christ: Where the exiles wept over Jerusalem's fall and cried for vengeance on their enemies, Christ wept over the very same city in its impenitence, Luke 19:41-44, and from the cross prayed for those who crucified Him, Luke 23:34. He bears the curse this psalm cries out for so that both the psalmist's grief and his enemies might find mercy at the cross, without ever softening the psalm's honest hatred of what evil actually does.
basic.god: God is trusted here as the only rightful judge of Babylon's cruelty. The psalm does not ask the exiles to execute vengeance themselves; it hands their unbearable grief and anger to the LORD, trusting Deuteronomy 32:35, Vengeance is Mine, I will repay, and Romans 12:19, which quotes it.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 13:16 describes exactly the atrocity the psalmist prays back upon Babylon. Luke 19:41-44 shows Jesus weeping over Jerusalem rather than cursing it. Romans 12:19 forbids personal vengeance and hands justice to God. Revelation 18:6 answers this psalm's imprecation, repay her as she herself has repaid, at the final judgment of Babylon the great.
basic.oneStory: This psalm is the Bible's rawest lament, exiles grieving a shattered Zion and crying out for God's own justice against documented cruelty. Its unanswered ache for home and its handed-over anger both find their resolution in Christ, who weeps over the city, absorbs the curse, and will one day judge every Babylon and bring His people home for good.

context.literary:
The psalm is a lament, but it is not built like most laments. There is no opening cry to God, no petition in the second person until verse 7, and no promise of praise at the end. It begins as a memory told in the first person plural, 'we sat and wept,' and it ends in a prayer so harsh that readers have argued over it for centuries. The movement is from past to future by way of a vow. Verses 1 to 4 look back to the rivers of Babylon. Verses 5 and 6 turn to the singer himself, with the pronoun suddenly singular, 'my right hand,' 'my tongue.' Verses 7 to 9 look forward and outward to Edom and Babylon.

Remembering and forgetting hold the poem together. The first verse says the exiles wept 'when we remembered Zion,' and the middle is an oath built on the same pair, forgetting and remembering, verses 5 and 6. In the Hebrew the same verb 'forget' stands in both halves of verse 5, 'If I forget you, O Jerusalem, may my right hand forget,' where the BSB has 'cease to function.' The final section then reverses the direction and asks God to remember, 'Remember, O LORD, the sons of Edom,' verse 7. A people who vow never to forget Jerusalem ask their God not to forget what was done to her.

There is a sharp use of place and music. The 'rivers of Babylon' are set against the 'river whose streams delight the city of God' in Psalm 46:4. The harps, hung up on the willows in verse 2, are the instruments of Zion's songs, and when the captors ask for 'a song of Zion' they are asking for something like Psalm 48 or Psalm 87, songs about the city the exiles saw burn. The refusal is the lament's centre. Finally, the repeated word 'blessed' in verses 8 and 9 stands where the Psalter's first word, in Psalm 1:1, also stands, which turns the ending into a dark echo of the Psalter's opening beatitude.
context.historical:
Nebuchadnezzar's army broke into Jerusalem in 586 BC. The temple was burned, the palace and 'every significant building' was destroyed, the walls were broken down, and the survivors were marched away, 2 Kings 25:8-12. Earlier deportations had taken others, and the exiles settled at places along Babylon's canals. Ezekiel was among them 'by the River Kebar,' Ezekiel 1:1, and 3:15 places the community at Tel-abib on the same river. The 'rivers of Babylon' are therefore not poetry for tears but the waterways of Mesopotamia, where a displaced people met to pray and to mourn.

The captors' demand is plausible. Conquerors often asked their captives for the songs of the homeland, whether for amusement or to humiliate them. The demand was cruel because the songs of Zion celebrated the very city that had just been destroyed and the God who was supposed to protect it. The psalm's reply, 'How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land?' is not stubbornness but grief. In the ancient world a god was tied to a land, and the exiles had to learn that the LORD was not. Jeremiah wrote to them to build houses, plant gardens and 'seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you,' Jeremiah 29:4-7, and told them that after seventy years God would restore them, Jeremiah 29:10.

Edom features in the psalm because of what its people did. Edom was Israel's brother nation, descended from Esau, Genesis 36:1. When Jerusalem fell, Obadiah says, Edom 'stood aloof,' 'gloated,' and 'looted' in 'the day of their disaster,' Obadiah 11-14, and stood at the crossroads to cut off fugitives. Lamentations 4:21-22 and Ezekiel 35:5 also accuse Edom of rejoicing. The psalm's phrase, 'the day Jerusalem fell,' echoes Obadiah's repeated 'day of.' Edom's cry, 'tear it down to its foundations,' has no other record, but it fits the pattern of an ally turned onlooker.

We cannot fix the psalm's date with certainty. The verbs in verse 1 are in the past tense, 'we sat and wept,' and 'there' appears twice, so some readers think the poem was written after the return, looking back. Others think it came out of the exile itself, as a fresh wound. The ending, with Babylon still standing as a 'Daughter of Babylon, doomed to destruction,' suggests it was before 539 BC, when Cyrus took Babylon and issued his decree, Ezra 1:1-4.
context.canonical:
Psalm 137 is the Psalter's chief witness to the exile from the inside. It stands in Book V, among psalms that have mostly moved from exile to return. Psalm 126 gives the answer to Psalm 137: 'When the LORD restored the captives of Zion, we were like dreamers. Then our mouths were filled with laughter, our tongues with shouts of joy,' Psalm 126:1-2. The harps that hung on the willows are taken down. Isaiah 52:9 says the same thing to the ruins of Jerusalem, 'Break forth in joy, sing together,' because 'the LORD has comforted His people.' Psalm 137 is the silence before those songs.

Its imprecation belongs with other prayers of the same kind. Psalm 79:1-4 grieves over the same fall of Jerusalem, and in verse 12 prays that the neighbours would be paid back sevenfold. Psalm 94:1-3 addresses 'O God of vengeance' and asks Him to 'shine forth.' Psalm 35, Psalm 69 and Psalm 139:19-22 are of the same family. The prophets also supply the answer in advance: Isaiah 13:16 and 13:19 foretold that Babylon's infants would be dashed to pieces and that the city would be overthrown, and Jeremiah 50:15 said, 'as she has done, do the same to her,' and 51:56 that 'the LORD is a God of retribution; He will repay in full.' The psalmist is asking God to do what God has said He will do.

The New Testament does not quote Psalm 137 but it hears it. Hebrews 11:13-16 describes the faithful as 'strangers and exiles on the earth' who long for 'a better country, a heavenly one,' and 1 Peter 1:1 and 2:11 call believers 'exiles' and 'foreigners.' Revelation turns 'Babylon' into the name of the world system that opposes God, Revelation 14:8 and 17:5, and in chapter 18 God's judgment falls on her in language that matches the psalm: 'Give back to her as she has done to others,' Revelation 18:6, and 'the sound of harpists and musicians ... will never ring out in you again,' Revelation 18:22. The martyrs under the altar cry, 'How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood?' Revelation 6:10.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted to preserve a memory and to keep a promise. The memory is of what happened, told without softening: the weeping, the mockery, the unbearable request for a song. The promise is the vow of verses 5 and 6, a self-curse by which he binds himself never to let Jerusalem fade from his mind or his hope. Exile is a threat to a people not only by what it takes but by what it tempts them to forget, and the psalm is written against forgetting. If the children grow up beside the canals of Babylon, they will need words that tell them where home is.

The ending is the most troubling part, and it was meant to be heard as prayer, not as policy. The psalmist turns to God and asks Him to remember Edom, and then he names Babylon's fate in terms that match its own deeds, 'repays you as you have done to us.' The intention is to hand vengeance to God and keep it out of human hands. A people with no army, no king and no city had nothing but the cry. The author makes sure that cry goes to the only court that could answer it, and does not cover over the rage that makes it necessary.

That is an act of faith. To pray this way is to believe that wrongs matter, that the God who made Zion is not indifferent to its destruction, and that He will not leave the cruelty of empires unanswered. The first hearers, still in Babylon or newly returned, were meant to feel permission to say all of it to God, and to leave it with Him.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes what exiles felt and said. It records the weeping, the silence of the harps, the oath, and the cry for justice. It is a model of honest prayer, but it is not a command for what anyone must feel or do. Nothing in it tells Israel to take up arms against Babylon or Edom, and nothing tells the church to wish harm on anyone. The speaker addresses God, and God alone, which is the decisive feature of the imprecation.

The abiding prescription is smaller and more demanding than a rule about vengeance. First, grief must be told to God, not hidden: Lamentations, the book of the same disaster, tells the people to 'pour out your heart like water in the presence of the Lord,' Lamentations 2:19. Second, justice belongs to God. Deuteronomy 32:35 says 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,' and Paul quotes it to forbid personal revenge, 'Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath,' Romans 12:19. Third, the proper response to enemies in the new covenant is stated by Jesus, 'love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,' Matthew 5:44.

These do not cancel the psalm. They fix its place. A believer who has been wronged can bring the whole of the anger to God, in the psalm's own words if need be, and then leave it there. What a believer may not do is take verse 9 as a model for treating anyone, and nobody should treat the psalm as a justification for violence against children. The psalm itself, by turning to God, closes that road.

debates.question: How should believers read the imprecation of verse 9, the blessing pronounced on whoever seizes Babylon's infants and brings them down on the rocks?

views.label: As raw, honest prayer that asks God to repay Babylon in kind
views.case: The verse is addressed to God and mirrors what Babylon's own kind of warfare did, Isaiah 13:16, and what the prophets said would come, so it asks for justice in the only form the speaker could picture.

views.label: As poetic hyperbole that makes Babylon's cruelty unbearable to hear
views.case: Hebrew poetry uses extreme language for effect. The verse may be meant to shock hearers into feeling the weight of the atrocity, not to specify an outcome.

views.label: As a prayer that the Bible allows to stand but not to be imitated
views.case: The psalm is in the canon so that the full range of human anguish is given a voice before God, but the New Testament's teaching on enemies, Matthew 5:44 and Romans 12:19-21, shows how it is to be handled now.

debates.bearing: On each reading the verse is prayer and not permission. It hands grief and anger to God, and it is to be read alongside Christ's own treatment of His enemies.

debates.question: Was the psalm written in Babylon or after the return?

views.label: In exile, as a fresh wound
views.case: The anger is raw, Babylon is still 'doomed to destruction,' and the demand for a song reads like an event that has just happened.

views.label: After the return, looking back
views.case: The verbs of verse 1 are past, 'there' is repeated, and the vow to remember Jerusalem makes the most sense for those who are no longer there and fear that distance will make them forget.

debates.bearing: The date does not change how the psalm is read. Whether new or remembered, it speaks for the people at the moment when grief is hardest to turn into praise.

debates.question: May Christians pray imprecatory psalms such as this one?

views.label: No, because Christ's command to love enemies replaces them
views.case: Matthew 5:44 and Luke 23:34 set a new pattern, and Stephen asks God not to hold his killers' sin against them, Acts 7:60. To pray for an enemy's destruction would contradict this.

views.label: Yes, as appeals to God's justice, with vengeance left to Him
views.case: Revelation 6:10 records the martyrs asking, 'How long ... until You avenge our blood?' and Paul in Romans 12:19 leaves room for God's wrath rather than forbidding the desire for justice. The psalms teach believers to bring their anger to God, not to hide it.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that the psalm gives no licence for human revenge. The difference is whether the prayer is still to be spoken, and the most careful use is to pray it for the world's evil, and to pray for enemies as persons, as Jesus did.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb that holds the psalm together is shakach, 'to forget.' In verse 5 it appears twice. The Hebrew says, in effect, 'If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget.' The BSB renders the second half as 'cease to function,' which is an interpretation of what the right hand would forget, probably its skill with the harp, since the harps were hung on the willows. The synonym in verse 6 is the verb zakar, 'remember,' which the lexicon notes, and the psalm turns on the contrast between the two. To forget is not just a lapse of memory but a failure of loyalty, and to remember is to act.

The oath in verse 6 says, 'May my tongue cling to the roof of my mouth,' using the verb dabaq, 'to cling or stick,' which is the same verb that Genesis 2:24 uses for a man who 'clings' to his wife. The singer asks that his mouth be glued shut, the musician's worst fate, if he does not remember. The last clause, 'if I do not exalt Jerusalem as my greatest joy,' is literally 'above the head of my joy,' al rosh simchati. Jerusalem is to be set at the summit of what makes him glad.

In verse 3 the captors ask for 'songs of joy.' The word translated 'tormentors' is rare in Hebrew, and its exact sense is uncertain, though it clearly refers to those who made the exiles suffer. What they ask for is 'a song of Zion,' shir Tsion, which seems to have been a recognised category of psalm, as in the songs that celebrate the city. The question in verse 4, 'How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land?' uses the phrase admat nekhar, 'foreign soil,' where nekhar means strange, alien, belonging to another.

Verse 7 has a doubled imperative: the Edomites cried 'Strip it, strip it,' in Hebrew 'aru 'aru, 'down to its foundations.' The doubling gives the mockery its sneer. The verb means to lay bare, and the foundation, yesod, is what remains when everything above has been torn off. In asking God to 'remember' what Edom said, the psalmist uses the covenant verb zakar, so that Edom's words are placed before God as evidence in a case.

The key legal word in verse 8 is the verb gamal and its noun gemul, repayment or deed. The line says, in effect, 'blessed is he who repays you your deed which you did to us.' The word gamal is used of dealing out good or ill, as in the weaning of a child or the recompense of an act, and here it is the language of a court. The principle behind it is the proportion found in the law, 'eye for eye, tooth for tooth,' Exodus 21:24, and Deuteronomy 19:21. In the Law that principle limited punishment to what the offence deserved. The psalm asks for exactly that, no more, though the shape of the repayment shocks.

Finally, 'blessed' in verses 8 and 9 is ashrei, the same word that begins the Psalter in Psalm 1:1, 'Blessed is the man,' and which the lexicon covers. Everywhere else in the Psalter it describes people who walk with God, trust Him, and live in His house. Here it appears twice, over the one who repays Babylon, and the reader notices the irony. The sense is not that the act itself is holy but that the person who is the instrument of God's justice against a cruel empire would be counted fortunate by those it had crushed. The word is a declaration of relief.

typology.fulfillment: The exiles longed for a home they could not reach and sang no songs in a foreign land. The New Testament says that all believers share this condition in Christ. Hebrews 11:13-16 describes the faithful as 'strangers and exiles on the earth' who long for 'a better country, a heavenly one,' and Peter calls the church 'exiles of the Dispersion,' 1 Peter 1:1, and 'foreigners and exiles,' 1 Peter 2:11. The escalation is that the homeland is no longer a rebuilt Jerusalem but 'the city that is to come,' Hebrews 13:14, and Paul says 'our citizenship is in heaven,' Philippians 3:20. The type falls short because the exiles were punished for their sin, while believers are exiles because they belong to another kingdom.

typology.type: Babylon as the city that opposes God
typology.fulfillment: Babylon became the Bible's picture of a human empire that exalts itself and crushes God's people. Revelation uses the name for the world system opposed to Christ, 'BABYLON THE GREAT,' Revelation 17:5, and proclaims 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great,' Revelation 14:8. The psalm's prayer that Babylon be repaid is answered in chapter 18, where she is told 'Give back to her as she has done to others,' Revelation 18:6, and the heavenly voice says 'God has pronounced for you His judgment against her,' Revelation 18:20. The type falls short because the historical Babylon fell to Cyrus and nothing changed in the deeper sense, while the final Babylon is overthrown by God and never rises again.

typology.type: Zion, the city that is remembered
typology.fulfillment: The psalmist's loyalty to Jerusalem looks beyond the earthly city. The prophets promise that Zion will be rebuilt and sing again, Isaiah 52:9, and the New Testament reveals that believers have already come 'to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem,' Hebrews 12:22, and will see 'the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God,' Revelation 21:2. The harps will be taken down, and the redeemed sing 'a new song,' Revelation 14:3. The type falls short because earthly Zion could be burned, while the heavenly city cannot.

study.christ:
Psalm 137 leads to Christ most clearly by contrast and by participation. The contrast is in how Jesus treated Jerusalem. The exiles wept over the city and then prayed for the ruin of its destroyers. Jesus also wept over Jerusalem, 'As Jesus approached Jerusalem and saw the city, He wept over it,' Luke 19:41, and told it what its enemies would do. But He did not pray for anyone's downfall. He said, 'If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace,' Luke 19:42, and elsewhere He longed to gather her children 'as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings,' Luke 13:34. His grief had the shape of the psalmist's grief, and its direction was mercy.

The participation is in exile. Jesus suffered 'outside the city gate,' Hebrews 13:12, and the writer invites believers to 'go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore.' The Son who was at home in the Father's house became a stranger in the world He made, John 1:10-11. On the cross He carried what the exiles carried: abandonment, mockery, and the apparent silence of God. Paul says He 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. The curse that the psalm calls down on Babylon falls on Him.

The psalm's cry for justice is answered, and not set aside, in the cross. Peter says of Jesus that 'when they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23. That is the psalm's own move of handing the matter to God, but carried to its end. He prayed, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,' Luke 23:34, and so the justice due to His enemies was absorbed in Him. Paul can then say that 'when we were enemies of God, we were reconciled to Him through the death of His Son,' Romans 5:10. The enemies the psalm names are not outside the reach of the one who bears the curse.

This does not mean the demand for justice is dropped. The Lamb who was slain is also the one who judges. The martyrs under the altar still ask how long, Revelation 6:10, and Babylon still falls, Revelation 18. The cross makes a way for the guilty to be forgiven if they turn, and it promises that those who do not will meet the judgment the psalm longs for, in the hands of the only Judge who can be trusted with it. The psalm cannot be allegorised as a hidden picture of Christ, but it is read in the light of Him: grief for the city, hatred of what evil does, and the refusal to take the sword.

There is a last hope. The exiles refused to sing in a foreign land, and the New Testament says that in Christ they will sing again. The new song of Revelation 14:3 is sung before the throne, and those who stand beside the sea of glass sing 'the song of God's servant Moses and of the Lamb,' Revelation 15:3. The harps hung on the willows come down at last.
study.god:
The psalm never says what the exiles thought about God's part in the disaster, but it shows a great deal about who they believed Him to be. He is the God of a place, Zion, and also the God they can address in a foreign land. The question 'How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land?' is not a denial that He is there. It is a lament that He seems to be absent, and the fact that the question is addressed to Him in a psalm shows that they still believed He could hear. Jeremiah had told them He could, Jeremiah 29:7, and the psalm is an act of faith in that word.

God is also the one who remembers. The psalm's two great verbs are 'forget' and 'remember.' The exiles vow not to forget Jerusalem, and they ask the LORD to remember Edom, which means to bring its deeds to account. A God who forgot would be of no use to people in their position. But a God who remembers is dangerous as well as comforting, because He remembers Judah's own sin as well as Babylon's cruelty. The psalm does not say this, but the Book of Lamentations and the prophets do, Lamentations 1:5, and the fall of Jerusalem is read there as a judgment. This psalm assumes it and still cries out, as a child cries out to a father who is also a judge.

The psalm also shows God as the righteous Judge of nations. The prayer in verse 8 assumes that Babylon will answer for what it has done, and the prophets confirm that God does hold empires to account, Jeremiah 25:12 and 51:56. The God of Psalm 137 is not neutral in the face of cruelty. He is a God to whom the wronged can appeal. The doctrine is hard, and it should be: Scripture insists that God's love for His people is not the whole of His character, and that His justice is the other side of His goodness, Exodus 34:7.

For worship, the psalm opens a place for honesty. It teaches that there are times when a believer cannot sing, and that the silence is itself something to bring to God. Worship does not require a mood. It requires truthful speech to the One who can hear, and the psalm gives that speech its own form. It also guards against the opposite danger. By placing vengeance in God's hands, it prevents the grief of the wronged from turning into the cruelty that wronged them. God is trusted with the one thing that human beings cannot safely hold, the final settling of accounts.

crossReferences.note: The answer to Psalm 137. When the LORD restored the captives of Zion, mouths filled with laughter and tongues with joy. The song that could not be sung by the rivers of Babylon is sung after the return, so the two psalms hold the whole story of the exile and its end.

The charge against Edom for standing aloof, gloating and looting 'in the day of their disaster.' It explains why Edom appears in verse 7 and shows the psalm's accusation to be a prophetic one, not a private grudge.

Edom is told to rejoice for now, because the cup will pass to her as well, while Zion's punishment is complete. It sets Edom's fate beside Jerusalem's and shows that the prayer of verse 7 was met by a prophetic promise of the same kind.

The prophet foretells the fall of Babylon, with its infants dashed to pieces before their eyes. It is the closest parallel to verse 9, and shows that the psalmist is asking for what a prophet already said God would do, in the grim language of war.

The letter to the exiles tells them to build, plant and seek the good of Babylon, because God would be with them there. It is the practical counterpart to the psalm: grief is real, but life in exile is to be lived faithfully, and the lament and the letter both belong to the same exile.

'The LORD is a God of retribution; He will repay in full.' Along with Jeremiah 50:15, 'as she has done, do the same to her,' this gives the theological basis of verse 8. Repayment is God's work, which is why the psalm addresses it to Him.

Paul quotes Deuteronomy 32:35 to forbid personal revenge and then says to feed the hungry enemy and 'overcome evil with good.' It is the New Testament's guide to using Psalm 137: justice is left to God, and the believer's own response is mercy.

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem as the exiles wept, and foretells her fall. Where the psalmist pleads for justice on Jerusalem's enemies, Jesus grieves for the city itself and for what it did not recognise, showing the shape of mourning that mercy takes.

'Give back to her as she has done to others.' The final Babylon's judgment repeats the psalm's logic of repayment in kind, and verse 22 adds that the sound of harpists will not be heard in her again, a reversal of the harps the exiles hung up.

The martyrs ask how long until God avenges their blood. It shows that the cry of Psalm 137 is not left behind in the New Testament. The saints still ask, and they are told to wait, so the prayer for justice is held within hope.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 137 is where the Bible's story of rebellion reaches its lowest point in the Old Testament. Genesis 3 began with a man and a woman driven out of a garden, and the long story that follows is, in one sense, a story of exile: Cain sent east of Eden, Babel scattered, Abraham called out of Ur, Israel in Egypt, and now Judah in Babylon. The rivers of Babylon recall the rivers of Eden, Genesis 2:10-14, but they are the rivers of a place where God's people do not belong. The psalm gives a voice to what the whole story has been moving toward and away from: the longing to be home.

It answers the question of what to do with grief and with anger at injustice in a fallen world. The world after Genesis 3 is full of cruelty that goes unanswered, and the psalm refuses both of the easy responses. It does not pretend the cruelty is small, and it does not say that the sufferers should take matters into their own hands. It brings everything to God, who has said that vengeance is His, Deuteronomy 32:35. That response sets up the New Testament's teaching in Romans 12:19, and it prepares for the One who will come, take the curse on Himself, and refuse to retaliate.

The story moves on through Cyrus, the return, and the rebuilt temple, Ezra 1:1-4, but the exile does not truly end there. The prophets promised more than a return, and the New Testament sees that Jesus is the one in whom the exile ends. He gathers the scattered, and the church lives as a people who are 'exiles' in the world and citizens of another city, Philippians 3:20. The question 'How can we sing the LORD's song in a foreign land?' is answered by the church's practice of singing in prison, in persecution and in ordinary Babylons, as Paul and Silas did, Acts 16:25.

The story ends with Babylon's fall and Zion's coming. Revelation 18 shows the great city overthrown, and chapter 21 shows the new Jerusalem coming down from God, where 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,' Revelation 21:4. The weeping by the rivers is finished, the harps are taken from the willows, and the demand for a song is replaced by a throne room in which the song is gladly sung. The vow of verse 6 is kept by God Himself, who has not forgotten Jerusalem, and the people who were remembered in their grief are brought home for good.

sermon.title: Praying Our Anger
sermon.why: Keller works through Psalm 137's searing pain and anger to show what to do with anger over serious mistreatment, both within the psalm's own logic and in light of the cross, making this the clearest trusted-cluster treatment of the psalm's hardest verses.

quiz.q: Why did the exiles hang their harps on the willows rather than sing?

options.text: Their captors mockingly demanded songs of joy, and grief made sacred song feel impossible in a foreign land.
options.note: Verses 2-4 show mockery and grief silencing worship, not mere sadness alone.

options.text: They had forgotten how to play their instruments.
options.note: The text says nothing about forgotten skill; it is grief and mockery that silence them.

options.text: Their harps had been physically destroyed by the Babylonians.
options.note: The harps are hung up, not destroyed; the point is refusal to perform sacred song for mockers.

options.text: They were commanded by God not to sing outside Jerusalem.
options.note: There is no such divine command; the psalm expresses the felt impossibility of singing amid mockery and grief.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist vow in verses 5-6?

options.text: Never to forget Jerusalem, even calling a curse on himself if he fails, showing covenant loyalty to Zion above every other joy.
options.note: The self-curse formula underscores how central Jerusalem was to the psalmist's identity and worship.

options.text: To take up arms and return to fight for Jerusalem immediately.
options.note: The vow is about memory and loyalty, not a call to military action.

options.text: To forgive Babylon completely and never think of Jerusalem's fall again.
options.note: This is the opposite of the text, which vows to remember, not to forget or move on.

options.text: To build a new temple in Babylon instead of Jerusalem.
options.note: The vow is exclusive loyalty to Jerusalem itself, not the founding of an alternative sanctuary.

quiz.q: Against whom does the psalmist specifically ask the LORD to remember wrongdoing in verse 7?

options.text: The sons of Edom, who cheered for Jerusalem's destruction on the day it fell.
options.note: Edom's betrayal, also condemned in Obadiah, is singled out alongside Babylon's cruelty.

options.text: The Assyrians who first threatened Jerusalem generations earlier.
options.note: The psalm addresses Edom and Babylon, contemporaries of the exile, not the earlier Assyrian threat.

options.text: The Egyptians who had enslaved Israel centuries before.
options.note: Egypt is not in view here; the psalm names Edom explicitly regarding Jerusalem's fall.

options.text: The prophets who had warned Judah of coming judgment.
options.note: The prophets are not being accused; the psalm targets nations that acted against Jerusalem, especially Edom.

quiz.q: How is the psalm's shocking final imprecation, verse 9, best understood?

options.text: As raw, honest prayer entrusting God's justice with Babylon's own documented cruelty, never a license for anyone to commit violence.
options.note: The verse is addressed to God as prayer, mirroring exactly the atrocities Babylon itself had inflicted, Isaiah 13:16.

options.text: As a straightforward command for believers to harm their enemies' children today.
options.note: This is a serious misreading; the verse is prayer handed to God, not instruction for human action, and stands against New Testament teaching, Romans 12:19.

options.text: As a later scribal error that should be removed from Scripture.
options.note: The verse is a genuine part of the inspired text and must be read within its lament and imprecatory genre, not excised.

options.text: As proof that the God of the Old Testament is fundamentally different from the God revealed in Christ.
options.note: The same God who hears this cry for justice is the God who, in Christ, both judges evil finally and offers mercy to sinners now.

quiz.q: How does Christ answer the ache and anger of this psalm?

options.text: He weeps over Jerusalem's coming judgment and prays for His enemies from the cross, absorbing the curse while never denying evil deserves judgment.
options.note: Luke 19:41-44 and Luke 23:34 show both grief over the city and mercy toward enemies converging in Christ.

options.text: He ignores the psalm entirely since it does not appear in the New Testament.
options.note: Its themes, weeping over Jerusalem, entrusting vengeance to God, and Babylon's judgment, are all taken up in the Gospels and Revelation.

options.text: He commands His followers to carry out the psalm's imprecation literally against Rome.
options.note: Jesus explicitly forbids retaliatory violence and instead prays for forgiveness for His enemies.

options.text: He promises that Jerusalem will never again face judgment of any kind.
options.note: Jesus in fact predicts further judgment on Jerusalem, Luke 19:43-44, even while weeping over it in love.

questions: The exiles could not sing the LORD's song in a foreign land. Where do you feel that same tension between grief and worship right now?
The psalmist vows never to forget Jerusalem above his greatest joy. What competes with Christ for the place of your greatest joy?
This psalm hands overwhelming anger over injustice to God rather than acting it out. What anger are you carrying that needs to be honestly prayed rather than either suppressed or acted upon?
Christ wept over the very city that would reject Him, and prayed for those who crucified Him. How does His example reshape the way you pray about people who have wronged you or those you love?
Revelation 18 promises that every Babylon will finally be judged. How does trusting God's future justice change how you carry present grief and anger today?

translationNotes.note: The BSB reads willows, with a footnote noting the Hebrew may also mean poplars, trees that commonly grew beside Babylon's canals and were well suited for hanging up unused instruments.
May my right hand cease to function renders a Hebrew idiom for the hand losing its skill or withering, a self-curse invoked if the psalmist ever forgets Jerusalem.

The verse mirrors, almost word for word, the kind of documented atrocity ancient conquerors like Babylon inflicted, Isaiah 13:16, so the prayer asks for measure-for-measure divine justice rather than inventing a new cruelty.
